(1) Do you remember the first book you read all by yourself? Maybe it was about a silly dog or a hungry caterpillar. Now you can help a younger student feel that same proud moment.
(2) This fall, Brookside Elementary is looking for sixth graders to become Reading Buddies. Buddies meet with a first grader for twenty minutes every Tuesday and Thursday during lunch.
(3) The program works. Ms. Patel, the reading coach at Brookside, has taught young readers for twelve years. She tracked last year's buddies and found that first graders who read with an older student finished the year reading about 30 more words per minute than those who did not.
(4) Buddies grow, too. Last year, sixth grader Leo Martinez was shy and rarely spoke in class. After reading with his buddy, Sam, every week, Leo says he feels braver about sharing ideas. "Sam cheers every time we finish a book," Leo said. "It's the best part of my week."
(5) Sign-up sheets are in the front office until September 20. Twenty minutes, twice a week, can change two readers' lives—a little one's and yours.
questions.stem: How does the story about Leo in paragraph 4 help persuade readers?
options: It shows how being a buddy can make an older student feel braver.
It gives the exact number of books Leo and Sam finished together.
It proves that every first grader reads faster after one year.
It explains why Ms. Patel chose Leo to be part of the program.
questions.why: Leo's story makes readers feel how the program helped a shy student grow, which supports the idea that "Buddies grow, too."

(1) Walking your dog at dusk? Riding your bike home from practice? Drivers need to see you, and BrightBand can help!
(2) BrightBand is a soft wristband with a strip that reflects car headlights. It slips on in seconds and fits any wrist.
(3) "I wear my BrightBand everywhere. It's the coolest thing ever!" says pop singer Jaylen Reyes, star of the hit song "Neon Nights."
(4) Officer Dana Brooks of the Millbrook Police Traffic Safety Unit has taught bike safety classes for ten years. "Reflective gear helps drivers spot people much sooner at night," she says. "That extra time can prevent a crash."
(5) In a test by the Millbrook Safety Council, drivers noticed walkers wearing reflective bands from about 500 feet away. Walkers in dark clothes without them were noticed from only about 100 feet away.
(6) Imagine your little brother crossing a dark street. Wouldn't you want every driver to see him?
(7) BrightBand comes in six colors for just $6. Each band is waterproof, so it keeps working in rain and snow. Get yours at Millbrook Hardware today. Be bright. Be seen. Be safe!
questions.stem: What effect does the question in paragraph 6 have on readers?
options: It reminds readers where they can go to buy the wristband.
It tells readers that the pop singer has a little brother.
It makes readers worry about someone they love getting hurt.
It gives readers a fact about how far drivers can see at night.
questions.why: Asking readers to imagine their little brother on a dark street stirs up worry and care, which makes them want to keep family members safe.

questions.passageTitle: Give Lost Things a Second Life
questions.passage:
Dear Principal Okafor,

(1) Every June, our lost-and-found bin is so full that the lid will not close. Last year, Mr. Patel, our head custodian for twelve years, counted 63 jackets, 41 water bottles, and 22 lunch boxes that nobody ever picked up. All of it was thrown away.

(2) I think we should donate these items instead. Picture a little boy waiting at the bus stop on a freezing January morning with no coat. One of our forgotten jackets could keep him warm all winter.

(3) The Harbor Street Clothing Closet has already agreed to take our donations. Its director, Ms. Lin, says that warm jackets are the item families ask for most.

(4) We could hold one "Last Chance Day" each month so students can claim their things first. After that, the class with the most helpers could win an extra library visit.

(5) Please help us give lost things a second life.

Sincerely,
Amira Haddad, Grade 5
questions.stem: Which detail from the letter would most convince a reader who wants proof that the lost-and-found problem is big?
options: the plan to hold a "Last Chance Day" for students every month
the count of 63 jackets, 41 bottles, and 22 lunch boxes
the picture of a boy waiting at a cold bus stop in January
the prize of an extra library visit for the class with the most helpers
questions.why: A reader who wants proof needs facts, and the exact count of unclaimed items shows how large the problem is. The other details are feelings, plans, or prizes, not proof.

questions.passageTitle: Let Fourth Graders Run the School Store
questions.passage:
Dear Principal Okafor,

(1) We, the students of Room 14, are asking you to let fourth graders run the school store on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

(2) Running the store would help us practice math every week. We would count money, make change, and keep track of what sells. Last spring, Room 12 ran a bake sale and raised $340 in two days. Their teacher, Mrs. Lin, said their mental math got faster that week.

(3) Mr. Haddad, who owned the Corner Mart on Main Street for 22 years, visited our class. He told us, "Running a shop teaches kids to be honest, careful, and polite."

(4) Most of all, we would feel proud. Think of how good it feels when someone trusts you with something important. We promise to be on time and to keep the store neat.

(5) Please give us a chance. We will not let you down.

Sincerely,
The Students of Room 14
questions.stem: How does paragraph 4 try to persuade the principal?
options: It quotes a shop owner who taught the class about money
It explains which days of the week the store would open
It gives numbers about how much money a store can earn
It asks her to remember how good it feels to be trusted
questions.why: "Think of how good it feels when someone trusts you" invites the principal to recall her own feelings. That feeling is meant to make her want to trust the students.

Dear Principal Okafor,
(1) Every night after the buses leave, the lights in many classrooms at Hillcrest Middle School stay on until morning. I am writing to ask that we turn them off before we go home.
(2) Leaving lights on wastes money. According to the Hillcrest District Facilities Office, our school spent about $4,200 last year to light empty rooms at night. That money could buy new books for the library or balls for the gym.
(3) Mr. Daniels, our head custodian, has taken care of this building for fifteen years. He told me that most rooms could be dark by 6:00 p.m. without causing any problems for the cleaning crew.
(4) Wasted light also hurts the creatures around us. Last spring, I found a tiny songbird lying still beneath our brightest window. Birds that fly at night can become confused by glowing buildings and crash into the glass.
(5) Turning off a switch takes one second. If each teacher flips the switch on the way out, and our student council puts a reminder sign by every door, we can save money and protect wildlife at the same time.
Sincerely,
Amira Haddad, Grade 6
questions.stem: How does the story about the songbird in paragraph 4 help persuade readers?
options: It gives exact facts about how many birds hit the school.
It shows that the author is an expert on night-flying birds.
It explains how much money the lights cost the school each night.
It makes readers feel sad about harm caused by the lights.
questions.why: Picturing a tiny bird lying still beneath the window makes readers feel sorry for the animals hurt by the bright lights. The story gives no counts or costs.

Dear Parent-Teacher Association,

(1) Room 12 is asking for $150 to buy a classroom fish tank. Here is why it is worth every penny.

(2) First, a fish tank would help us learn science. In fifth grade, we study ecosystems. Instead of only reading about how plants, animals, and water work together, we could watch it happen every day.

(3) Second, fish can help students feel calm. Dr. Helen Marsh, a children's doctor at Brookside Clinic, explains that watching fish swim for a few minutes can slow a person's heartbeat. "It is like a short rest for the mind," she says.

(4) Third, caring for fish teaches responsibility. Each week, two students would feed the fish and test the water.

(5) Last month, our classmate Jonah was nervous before the state test. He told us he wished there were something peaceful to look at. When we visited Room 9's tank, his shoulders relaxed and he smiled for the first time all morning.

(6) Please give our class the chance to grow, learn, and care. Thank you!

Sincerely,
The Students of Room 12
questions.stem: Which detail best supports the reason that a fish tank would help students learn science?
options: Students could watch plants, animals, and water work together every day.
Jonah relaxed and smiled when the class visited Room 9's tank.
Dr. Marsh says that watching fish swim for a few minutes can slow a heartbeat.
Two students would feed the fish and test the water every week.
questions.why: The class studies ecosystems, and watching living things and water work together connects the tank to that science lesson. The other details support different reasons, such as feeling calm or learning responsibility.

(1) Field Day is coming on May 20! There will be sack races, a tug-of-war, and a water balloon toss. But before you run outside, remember one more thing: sunscreen.

(2) Dr. Lena Park is a skin doctor at Riverbend Clinic. She says, "Just one bad sunburn as a child can hurt your skin for years. I tell every family to use sunscreen, even on cloudy days."

(3) Last year, the school nurse treated 23 sunburns after Field Day. That is almost one student from every class!

(4) A sunburn can turn a happy day into a painful night. Picture trying to sleep when your shoulders burn every time you roll over.

(5) Sunscreen takes only one minute to put on. Pack a bottle in your bag, and put it on before you go outside. Then enjoy the fun!

options: It makes readers imagine a sunburn's pain so they want to avoid one
It gives readers a number that shows how common sunburns can be
It makes readers excited about the games planned for Field Day
It tells readers exactly how long it takes to put on their sunscreen
questions.why: Asking readers to picture burning shoulders at bedtime helps them feel the pain. That feeling makes them want to wear sunscreen.

questions.passageTitle: A Reading Dog for Willow Creek? A Debate
questions.passage:
Opening Statement For: Ms. Carla Diaz, School Counselor

(1) I have been a school counselor for sixteen years, and I have never seen anything calm a nervous reader as quickly as a dog does. Today I ask you to bring a trained therapy dog to Willow Creek Elementary once a week.

(2) The Tri-County Reading Project paired 120 struggling second through fifth graders with therapy dogs for one semester. Their reading fluency grew by an average of 12 percent, compared with 4 percent for students who read aloud to adults.

(3) Dogs do not correct, sigh, or laugh. As one fourth grader in the project said, "Biscuit doesn't care if I mess up. He just listens."

(4) The dog and its handler would be certified by Paws for Learning, an organization that tests every dog for calm behavior around children.

Opening Statement Against: Jordan Ellis, Student Council

(1) Everyone loves dogs, including me. But a school program has to work for every student, not just most of them.

(2) According to our school nurse, 23 Willow Creek students have documented pet allergies, and 6 of them have asthma that allergens can trigger. Dog hair travels on clothes and backpacks, so a dog in the library would affect the whole building, not just one room.

(3) Imagine being the one student in your class who has to sit in the office while everyone else reads with the dog. You would feel left out every single week.

(4) Instead, we could start a reading buddy program that pairs fifth graders with younger students. It costs nothing, and no one is left out.
questions.stem: A parent at the meeting cares most about whether the program will actually raise reading scores. Which part of the debate would most likely persuade this parent?
options: the fourth grader's words about how Biscuit just listens
Ellis's description of a student sitting alone in the office
the news that Paws for Learning tests every dog's behavior
Diaz's comparison of 12 percent growth with 4 percent growth
questions.why: This parent wants proof that reading improves, and the Tri-County comparison shows much larger fluency growth with dogs. The other parts address feelings or safety, not results.

questions.passageTitle: Every School Day Needs a Nurse
questions.passage:
(1) On Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, Kendall Middle School has a full-time nurse. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, it has a locked office and a sign that says "Call the front desk." Our 640 students deserve a nurse every day of the week.
(2) Health problems do not follow a schedule. According to the Kendall County Health Department, about one in eleven students in our county has asthma, and dozens more at our school have serious food allergies or diabetes. These students can need help at any moment, not just on the three days the nurse is here.
(3) When the nurse is gone, office workers do their best, but they are not trained medical staff. Last February, a seventh grader had an asthma attack on a Thursday. The secretary, who had never used an inhaler spacer, had to read the instructions while the student struggled to breathe. Luckily, he recovered. Next time, we may not be so lucky.
(4) Nurse Grace Allen, who has worked in school health for eighteen years and holds a state school nurse license, says the problem goes beyond emergencies. "I see students for headaches that turn out to be vision problems, or stomachaches that come from stress," she explains. "When I'm not here, those clues get missed."
(5) A full-time nurse also keeps students in class. Last year, on days the nurse was present, about 3 percent of students who visited the office were sent home. On days she was absent, that number jumped to 11 percent, because office staff had no way to judge whether a student was truly sick.
(6) Adding two more days of nursing would cost the district about $26,000 a year. That is less than the cost of one new school bus.
(7) Please contact the Kendall School Board before its March 4 meeting and ask it to fund a nurse every day. Our health shouldn't depend on what day of the week it is.
questions.stem: The author wants to add one more detail to paragraph 6. Which detail would be most relevant to the point made there?
options: The number of years Nurse Allen has worked at Kendall
The added cost per student, which is about $40 a year
The number of students who ride a school bus every morning
A description of the medical supplies kept in the nurse's office
questions.why: Paragraph 6 argues that the cost is reasonable, so breaking $26,000 into a small amount per student adds logical support to that exact point.

(1) On Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, Kendall Middle School has a full-time nurse. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, it has a locked office and a sign that says "Call the front desk." Our 640 students deserve a nurse every day of the week.
(2) Health problems do not follow a schedule. According to the Kendall County Health Department, about one in eleven students in our county has asthma, and dozens more at our school have serious food allergies or diabetes. These students can need help at any moment, not just on the three days the nurse is here.
(3) When the nurse is gone, office workers do their best, but they are not trained medical staff. Last February, a seventh grader had an asthma attack on a Thursday. The secretary, who had never used an inhaler spacer, had to read the instructions while the student struggled to breathe. Luckily, he recovered. Next time, we may not be so lucky.
(4) Nurse Grace Allen, who has worked in school health for eighteen years and holds a state school nurse license, says the problem goes beyond emergencies. "I see students for headaches that turn out to be vision problems, or stomachaches that come from stress," she explains. "When I'm not here, those clues get missed."
(5) A full-time nurse also keeps students in class. Last year, on days the nurse was present, about 3 percent of students who visited the office were sent home. On days she was absent, that number jumped to 11 percent, because office staff had no way to judge whether a student was truly sick.
(6) Adding two more days of nursing would cost the district about $26,000 a year. That is less than the cost of one new school bus.
(7) Please contact the Kendall School Board before its March 4 meeting and ask it to fund a nurse every day. Our health shouldn't depend on what day of the week it is.
questions.stem: Why does the author mention Nurse Allen's eighteen years of experience and her state license?
options: To prove that she wrote the county's report about student asthma
To show that she has worked at Kendall longer than other staff
To show that her view about missed health clues can be trusted
To explain why she is able to work only three days each week
questions.why: Her training and long experience make her a credible source for the claim that headaches and stomachaches can be clues to bigger problems.

questions.passageTitle: Fix the Sidewalks on Harper Road
questions.passage:
(1) Good evening, members of the Linwood City Council. My name is Nadia Farouk, and I am a sixth grader at Harper Road Middle School. Every morning, more than 200 students walk to school along Harper Road. Tonight I am asking you to repair its sidewalks.
(2) The sidewalk between Oak Lane and the school entrance is cracked, tilted, and in some places missing completely. Where the concrete has crumbled, students step into the street to get around the holes. Cars on Harper Road travel at 35 miles per hour, just a few feet away.
(3) These are not small bumps. Last October, my friend Tomás tripped over a raised slab of concrete while carrying his science project. He broke his wrist, and his volcano model—three weeks of work—was smashed on the pavement. He spent the rest of the semester writing with his left hand.
(4) Tomás is not the only one. According to the school nurse's records, nine students were treated last year for injuries from falls on the way to school. Seven of those falls happened on Harper Road.
(5) The city already knows about the problem. Linwood's Public Works Department rated this sidewalk "poor" in its 2025 street survey, the lowest rating it gives. The same report estimated that repairs would cost about $48,000. That may sound like a lot, but the city spent more than that last year repainting the lines in the downtown parking garage.
(6) Some people say students should simply be more careful. But no amount of care can fix a sidewalk that disappears. When the safe path ends, children have only two choices: climb over broken concrete or walk next to traffic.
(7) You have the power to give 200 students a safe walk to school. Please vote to fund the Harper Road repairs this year—before someone else gets hurt.
questions.stem: How does paragraph 4 strengthen the argument begun by the story in paragraph 3?
options: It shows that Tomás's fall was part of a pattern, not a single accident.
It shows that the school nurse was the first to report the broken sidewalk.
It explains the reasons the city rated the sidewalk as "poor" in 2025.
It proves that Tomás's injury was more serious than the other injuries.
questions.why: One story might be bad luck, but the nurse's records show seven falls on Harper Road, adding reasoned evidence that the problem is ongoing.

(1) Do you like puzzles, secret plans, and surprise endings? Then the Hilltop Chess Club is waiting for you. We meet every Wednesday from 3:00 to 4:15 in Room 22.

options: It asks readers whether they enjoy puzzles and secret plans
It describes how nervous a new member felt on her first day
It promises that the club will lend boards to practice at home
It gives numbers showing most members improved in reading
questions.why: Nineteen of 26 members moved up a reading level. That fact speaks to readers who want a school benefit.

questions.passageTitle: Keep Music Class Twice a Week
questions.passage:
(1) Good evening, members of the Lakeview School Board. My name is Priya Shah, and I am in fourth grade at Lakeview Elementary. I am here to ask you not to cut music class from twice a week to once a week.

(2) When my grandmother moved in with us, she could not speak much English, and I could not speak much Gujarati. But we both knew the song "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." The first night she lived with us, we sang it together, and she laughed and hugged me. Music gave us a way to talk before we had the words.

(3) Music also helps students in other subjects. Our music teacher, Ms. Carver, has taught for 18 years and has a master's degree in music education. She explained that reading music uses fractions, because notes are split into halves, quarters, and eighths.

(4) Numbers back this up. Last year, the Lakeview District Report found that fourth graders who took music twice a week scored 9 points higher on the spring math test than those who took it once a week.

(5) I know the board needs to save money. But a year of music class costs less than one new set of math textbooks, and it helps students in math anyway.

(6) Please keep music twice a week. Do it for every student who has ever found a friend, or a grandmother, through a song.
questions.stem: How does paragraph 5 help persuade board members who care most about cost?
options: It describes how a song helped Priya talk with her grandmother
It explains that musical notes are divided into fraction parts
It reports that students who took more music had higher scores
It shows music costs less than textbooks yet still helps math
questions.why: Priya admits the board needs to save money, then argues music is cheap and still improves math. That answers a cost-focused member directly.

questions.passageTitle: Let Us Pick Our Own Books
questions.passage:
(1) Imagine being handed a book about a topic you find boring and being told you must read it for the next three weeks. For many students at Westbrook Elementary, this is what reading class feels like.

(2) Our school should let students choose at least half of the books they read in class. When readers pick their own books, they read more. A survey by the Westbrook Reading Council found that students who chose their own books read an average of 24 minutes a night, compared to 11 minutes for students who were assigned books.

(3) Reading expert Dr. Paul Nguyen, who has studied young readers for 25 years, agrees. "Choice is the spark," he writes. "Children who choose become children who read for fun."

(4) Some people worry that students will choose only easy books. However, teachers can still guide students with a list of good choices at different levels. Students would still read challenging books; they would just have a say in which ones.

(5) I know this works because it happened to me. In fourth grade, my teacher let me pick a book about deep-sea creatures. I stayed up late with a flashlight, reading about glowing fish and giant squid. For the first time, I couldn't wait to get to reading class.

(6) Books can open doors to whole new worlds, but only if students want to walk through them. Let's give every student the key.

Sofia Marquez, Grade 5 Reporter, The Westbrook Weekly

options: It explains why teachers should create reading lists for students at many different levels.
It shares a personal memory so readers feel the excitement that choice can bring.
It shows that students should be allowed to read late at night with flashlights.
It gives numbers that show how many students prefer books about the ocean.
questions.why: The author's memory of staying up late with a book about sea creatures helps readers feel how exciting it is to read a chosen book. It is a story, not statistics.

questions.passage:
(1) Good evening, members of the council. My name is Marcus Bell, and I am in fifth grade at Harmon Road Elementary.

(2) Every morning, I watch my little sister grip her backpack straps as cars rush past our bus stop. She is only six. Sometimes she asks me, "Will the cars stop for us today?" No child should have to ask that question.

(3) This is not just a feeling. The Millbrook Police Department measured traffic on Harmon Road for two weeks in March. The speed limit is 25 miles per hour, but the average car near our stop was going 38. In the past year, there have been 4 accidents within one block of the school.

(4) Officer Tanya Brooks, who has worked as a school safety officer in Millbrook for fifteen years, told our class that a flashing crosswalk sign is "one of the simplest ways to make drivers slow down." She said she has seen these signs work at three other schools in our county.

(5) A flashing sign costs about $9,000. That may sound like a lot, but it is less than the town spent on new holiday decorations last year.

(6) You have the power to protect the youngest people in our town. Please vote yes on the crosswalk sign. My sister, and every child at our stop, is counting on you.

Thank you.

(1) At Fairhaven Middle School, the first bell rings at 7:25 a.m. For many students, that means waking up before 6:00, while it is still dark outside. Our school board should move the start time to 8:30.
(2) Teenagers' bodies are not built for early mornings. Dr. Helen Cho, a sleep scientist who has studied adolescent sleep for over twenty years at Westbrook University, explains that during the preteen and teen years, the body's internal clock shifts later. "Asking a twelve-year-old to be alert at 7:00 a.m. is like asking an adult to be alert at 5:00 a.m.," she says.

(4) My older cousin, who goes to a school that starts at 8:45, says she loves it and feels great every day.
(5) Picture a sixth grader at 7:30 a.m., trying to solve a math problem while her eyes keep closing. She knows the answer is somewhere in her mind, but she cannot reach it. She is not lazy. She is exhausted.
(6) Some parents worry that a later start will make it hard to drop children off on the way to work. This is a real concern. The school could open the library at 7:30 for students who need to arrive early, so families would have a safe place to send them.
(7) Changing a bell schedule is not easy, but the evidence is clear. A later start would give students the sleep their growing bodies need. Board members, please give our students the chance to start the day awake.

(1) Members of the Planning Board, the city plans to cut down the 200-year-old oak tree on Pine Street to widen the road by six feet. I am here to ask you to save it.

(2) That oak was already tall when our town was founded. My grandfather asked my grandmother to marry him under its branches in 1968. Last spring, my class sat in its shade and sketched the robins nesting in it. When I imagine a stump where that tree stands, I feel like our town is losing a piece of its memory.

(3) The oak also does real work. According to the Greenfield Tree Society, a tree this size soaks up about 4,000 gallons of rainwater a year, which helps keep Pine Street from flooding. It also shades the sidewalk, which can make the ground beneath it up to 20 degrees cooler on summer afternoons.

(4) City arborist Dr. Leon Fischer, who has cared for Greenfield's trees for 18 years, inspected the oak in May. He reported that it is healthy and "could easily live another hundred years."

(5) Some people say widening the road will help traffic. But the city's own traffic report shows that Pine Street has backups for only about ten minutes each morning. Six extra feet of road will not change much.

(6) There is a better choice. The city could add a turning lane at the Main Street corner, two blocks away, where most of the morning backups actually begin. That plan would fix the real problem without cutting down a single tree.

(7) Also, my neighbor says she once heard that cutting down big trees makes nearby home prices drop by half. That is a lot of money!

(8) A road can be repaved anytime. A 200-year-old tree cannot be replaced in our lifetimes. Please vote to keep the Pine Street Oak standing.

Speech by Nadia Kowalski, Grade 5, at the Greenfield Planning Board meeting

questions.passageTitle: Should School Start Later? Two Views
questions.passage:
Text A: "Let Our Mornings Start Later" by Jonah, Grade 4

(1) Every morning at 6:15, my alarm rings, and I feel like I am being pulled out of a warm lake. I stumble to the bus stop in the dark. By second period, my eyes are heavy, and the words in my book swim around the page. Lots of my classmates feel the same way.

(2) Dr. Helen Brooks, a sleep doctor at Maplewood Children's Hospital who has studied children's sleep for 25 years, says that children ages 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. "Tired children are not lazy," she says. "Their brains simply have not had time to rest."

(3) If school started at 8:45 instead of 7:45, we would arrive awake, ready, and maybe even smiling. Isn't that the kind of school we all want?

Text B: "Why 7:45 Still Works" by Diane Ferris, Maplewood Transportation Director

(1) I understand that early mornings can be hard. But moving the start time would cause serious problems.

(2) Maplewood's 14 buses each make two trips: one for the elementary schools and one for the middle and high schools. If elementary school started an hour later, the district would need 9 more buses and drivers. According to the district budget office, that would cost about $480,000 a year.

(3) A later start would also mean a later end. Students would get home after 4:00, leaving less daylight for sports and play in the winter. In a survey of 600 Maplewood families, 61 percent said a later end time would make it harder for them to pick up their children.

(4) There are cheaper ways to help tired students, such as earlier bedtimes and less screen time at night.

"Tired children are not lazy."
questions.why: A member focused on the budget will care most about a large yearly cost. The other details concern feelings, sleep, or daylight, not money.

questions.passageTitle: Turn Down the Lights, Turn Up the Stars
questions.passage:
Dear Members of the Cedar Falls Town Council,

(1) Last summer, my family went camping at Lost Pine Lake, two hours away from town. When the campfire went out, I looked up and gasped. The sky was so full of stars that it looked like someone had spilled sugar across a black tablecloth. Back home in Cedar Falls, I can count the stars I see from my backyard on two hands. I am writing to ask the council to change the lights on our streets so that every child in our town can see a sky like that.

(2) Our streetlights shine light in every direction, including straight up into the sky, where no one needs it. Covered lights, called "shielded" lights, point the light down at the sidewalk instead. Mr. Arturo Diaz, who has led the Cedar Falls Astronomy Club for 30 years, says, "With shielded lights, our town could see five times as many stars on a clear night."

(3) Shielded lights save money, too. When the town of Brook Valley switched 800 streetlights to shielded LED lights in 2023, its yearly electric bill for streetlights dropped from $210,000 to $96,000, according to the Brook Valley Public Works Office.

(4) Bright lights at night also confuse animals. Baby sea turtles, for example, crawl toward lights instead of toward the ocean. Even though we don't have sea turtles here, our owls, moths, and bats need the dark too.

(5) Some people worry that shielded lights will make streets less safe. But shielded lights still light up sidewalks and roads, the places people actually walk and drive. They simply stop wasting light on the sky.

(6) Please vote to replace our streetlights with shielded lights. Let's give the stars back to Cedar Falls.

Sincerely,
Nadia Kareem, Grade 4, Cedar Falls Elementary

options: Paragraph 5, because it explains that the roads would still be lit
Paragraph 1, because it describes the beautiful sky at Lost Pine Lake
Paragraph 2, because a club leader says the town would see more stars
Paragraph 3, because another town cut its light bill by over half
questions.why: Brook Valley's bill fell from $210,000 to $96,000. That savings is exactly what a budget-minded council member wants to hear.

(1) Every afternoon at 2:45, a long line of cars wraps around Pinecrest Elementary. Most of them sit with their engines running for ten, fifteen, even twenty minutes. Parents may not realize it, but that running engine is filling the air our children breathe.

(2) Car exhaust contains gases and tiny particles that can make it harder to breathe. Dr. Amina Shah, a lung doctor at Valley Children's Hospital, warns that children are "especially at risk because they breathe faster than adults and their lungs are still growing." She has treated hundreds of children with asthma, and she calls pickup-line idling "a problem we can easily fix."

(3) Turning off your engine also saves money. According to the Valley Clean Air Office, a car that idles for 10 minutes a day wastes about 27 gallons of gas a year. That adds up to about $90, just for sitting still.

(4) Last fall, our Green Team students counted idling cars for one week. On Monday, 46 out of 60 cars had their engines running. After we put up signs and handed out reminder cards, only 12 out of 60 cars were idling by Friday.

(5) Think about the kindergartners walking past those tailpipes, holding hands with their buddies, their small faces right at the level of the exhaust. They cannot choose what air they breathe. You can choose for them.

(6) Next time you wait for pickup, turn the key. It only takes a second, and it makes a difference that lasts.

Posted by the Pinecrest Green Team

options: It explains that idling cars can cause asthma in young children.
It shows them how many cars at Pinecrest idle every afternoon.
It describes how the Green Team made signs and reminder cards.
It shows them that turning off the engine will save them money.
questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives a different reason to stop idling: about $90 in wasted gas each year. That reason can reach parents who are not moved by health concerns.

questions.passageTitle: A Reading Dog for Willow Creek? A Debate
questions.passage:
Opening Statement For: Ms. Carla Diaz, School Counselor

(1) I have been a school counselor for sixteen years, and I have never seen anything calm a nervous reader as quickly as a dog does. Today I ask you to bring a trained therapy dog to Willow Creek Elementary once a week.

(2) The Tri-County Reading Project paired 120 struggling second through fifth graders with therapy dogs for one semester. Their reading fluency grew by an average of 12 percent, compared with 4 percent for students who read aloud to adults.

(3) Dogs do not correct, sigh, or laugh. As one fourth grader in the project said, "Biscuit doesn't care if I mess up. He just listens."

(4) The dog and its handler would be certified by Paws for Learning, an organization that tests every dog for calm behavior around children.

Opening Statement Against: Jordan Ellis, Student Council

(1) Everyone loves dogs, including me. But a school program has to work for every student, not just most of them.

(2) According to our school nurse, 23 Willow Creek students have documented pet allergies, and 6 of them have asthma that allergens can trigger. Dog hair travels on clothes and backpacks, so a dog in the library would affect the whole building, not just one room.

(3) Imagine being the one student in your class who has to sit in the office while everyone else reads with the dog. You would feel left out every single week.

(4) Instead, we could start a reading buddy program that pairs fifth graders with younger students. It costs nothing, and no one is left out.
questions.stem: How does Ms. Diaz's first sentence prepare listeners to accept the rest of her argument?
options: It shows that the school has already tried a dog program and found it worked.
It shows her long experience with students, so her later claims seem trustworthy.
It shows that she owns a therapy dog and has trained it herself to work with young readers.
It shows that she has studied the Tri-County Reading Project for sixteen years.
questions.why: By opening with sixteen years as a counselor, Ms. Diaz tells listeners she knows students well, so they are more likely to trust what she says next. Nothing says she owns a dog or ran the study.

questions.passageTitle: Learn First Aid Before You Need It
questions.passage:
(1) Last October, my little brother Leo fell off the monkey bars and cut his arm. There was blood everywhere, and everyone around us froze. Everyone except my friend Aisha. She had taken a first aid class at the community center, so she knew to press a clean cloth on the cut and keep pressing while someone ran for a teacher. Later, the nurse told us that Aisha had done exactly the right thing.

(2) That day, I realized something: grown-ups are not always right next to us when someone gets hurt. That is why I believe every fourth grader at Oakridge Elementary should take a short first aid class.

(3) The class would not take much time. The Oakridge Red Cross Chapter offers a free two-hour "Kids Can Help" class that teaches how to clean small cuts, what to do for a nosebleed, and how to call 911 and give an address clearly.

(4) Experts agree that children can learn these skills. Paramedic Carla Mendes has answered emergency calls for 16 years. "Some of the best 911 callers I've ever heard were children," she says. "When kids are taught what to say, they stay calmer and help us get there faster."

(5) Other schools have already tried it. At Pine Ridge Elementary, every fourth grader took the class in 2024. Afterward, 88 percent of them could correctly answer five out of five first aid questions, compared with 21 percent before the class.

(6) Some people say fourth graders are too young to handle an emergency. But Aisha was nine years old. She did not panic, because she knew what to do.

(7) Two hours is a small price for a skill that could last a lifetime. Let's make sure the next time someone gets hurt, nobody freezes.
questions.stem: A reader says, "A story about one kid doesn't prove anything. I want to hear from someone whose job is handling emergencies." Which sentence would best answer this reader?
options: "When kids are taught what to say, they stay calmer and help us get there faster."
"The Oakridge Red Cross Chapter offers a free two-hour 'Kids Can Help' class..."
"Afterward, 88 percent of them could correctly answer five out of five first aid questions..."
"She did not panic, because she knew what to do."
questions.why: These are the words of a paramedic with 16 years of answering emergency calls. The test result is strong evidence, but it does not come from a person whose job is handling emergencies.

(1) Good afternoon, judges and classmates. Our team argues that Sunridge Middle School should add a robotics elective for sixth through eighth graders next year.
(2) First, robotics teaches skills students will need. The state Department of Labor projects that jobs in engineering and computer science in our state will grow by about 15 percent over the next ten years—more than twice as fast as jobs overall. In a robotics class, students write code, test designs, and fix mistakes, which are the same steps engineers use every day.
(3) Second, robotics reaches students who don't always shine in traditional classes. Mr. Alvarez, who has coached the Sunridge after-school robotics club for six years, has noticed that some of his most dedicated builders are students who struggle in math class. "When they see a gear turn because of a number they calculated," he says, "math suddenly matters."
(4) Third, the club can't meet the demand. This year, 85 students applied for the club's 20 spots. Sixty-five students were turned away.
(5) Fourth, robotics is simply awesome. Robots are the future, and everyone knows that the coolest kids are the ones who build them.
(6) Our opponents will say the school cannot afford new equipment. However, the Sunridge Education Foundation has offered a $10,000 grant for the first year, which would pay for fifteen robot kits that can be reused for at least five years.
(7) Last spring, I watched my classmate Ana, who barely spoke in class, stand in front of 300 people at the regional competition and explain how her team's robot worked. Her voice shook at first, but by the end, she was grinning. Every student at Sunridge deserves a chance to find their voice the way Ana did.
(8) Some may ask whether students would really choose this class. A survey by our student council found that 62 percent of the 300 sixth and seventh graders who responded would sign up for a robotics elective if it were offered. That is far more than the fifteen kits could serve in a single section, so the school could even offer two sections each year.
(9) For all these reasons, we urge you to support a robotics elective at Sunridge.

His opinion is backed up by the Department of Labor's data about future jobs.

(5) Some people say widening the road will help traffic. But the city's own traffic report shows that Pine Street has backups for only about ten minutes each morning. Six extra feet of road will not change much.

(6) There is a better choice. The city could add a turning lane at the Main Street corner, two blocks away, where most of the morning backups actually begin. That plan would fix the real problem without cutting down a single tree.

(7) Also, my neighbor says she once heard that cutting down big trees makes nearby home prices drop by half. That is a lot of money!

(8) A road can be repaved anytime. A 200-year-old tree cannot be replaced in our lifetimes. Please vote to keep the Pine Street Oak standing.

Both paragraphs use numbers to show how much money the city would lose without the tree.
Paragraph 2 gives a tree expert's opinion; paragraph 3 tells a story about the speaker's own family.
Paragraph 2 explains the traffic problem; paragraph 3 describes the city's plan to fix it.
questions.why: Paragraph 2 uses family memories and the class's sketching trip to build feeling, and paragraph 3 adds facts about flooding and shade. Together they appeal to both the heart and the mind.

questions.passageTitle: Should Pinecrest Ban Fireworks? Two Speeches
questions.passage:
Speech A: "Quiet Skies for Everyone" by Daniel Osei, volunteer at Pinecrest Animal Rescue
(1) Each July, the night sky over Pinecrest fills with booms and crackles. For many of us, it is a celebration. For others, it is a nightmare.
(2) I have volunteered at the Pinecrest Animal Rescue for nine years. Every July 5th, our phones ring nonstop. Last year, we took in 37 lost dogs in the three days after the holiday—more than we usually see in a month. One was a gray terrier named Biscuit, found shivering under a car four miles from home, his paws raw from running.
(3) Pets are not the only ones affected. Veterans living with trauma and young children with sensory sensitivities can find sudden explosions terrifying.
(4) The Pinecrest Fire Department reported 14 fires caused by fireworks last summer, including one that destroyed a garage on Cedar Street.
(5) I'm not asking Pinecrest to give up celebrating. I'm asking us to switch to a professional drone light show, which the nearby town of Ashby held last year with no noise and no fires. Let's celebrate in a way that welcomes everyone.

Speech B: "Keep Our Tradition Bright" by Laila Mansour, owner of Mansour Family Fireworks
(1) Fireworks have lit up Pinecrest every summer for more than eighty years. My grandfather sold the first ones from a wooden stand on Main Street.
(2) A ban would hurt our town. Fireworks sales bring thousands of visitors to Pinecrest every July, and those visitors buy meals, gas, and souvenirs. Everyone I talk to says the Fourth wouldn't be the same without them.
(3) Some people say fireworks are dangerous. But anyone can be careless with anything. The answer is safety education, not a ban.
(4) Ask yourself: do we really want to tell our children that the magic they felt watching the sky light up is gone forever?
(5) Let's keep the tradition that makes Pinecrest special.
questions.stem: Which addition would most strengthen Mansour's paragraph 3 for listeners who are worried about fires?
options: A question asking listeners how they felt watching fireworks as children
A list of the most popular fireworks that her family's shop sells each year
A story about her grandfather's first fireworks stand on Main Street
Data showing fireworks fires dropped in towns that offered safety classes
questions.why: Mansour claims safety education is the answer but gives no proof. Evidence that safety classes reduced fires would directly answer Osei's fire statistics.

questions.passageTitle: Should School Start Later? Two Views
questions.passage:
Text A: "Let Our Mornings Start Later" by Jonah, Grade 4

(1) Every morning at 6:15, my alarm rings, and I feel like I am being pulled out of a warm lake. I stumble to the bus stop in the dark. By second period, my eyes are heavy, and the words in my book swim around the page. Lots of my classmates feel the same way.

(2) Dr. Helen Brooks, a sleep doctor at Maplewood Children's Hospital who has studied children's sleep for 25 years, says that children ages 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. "Tired children are not lazy," she says. "Their brains simply have not had time to rest."

(3) If school started at 8:45 instead of 7:45, we would arrive awake, ready, and maybe even smiling. Isn't that the kind of school we all want?

Text B: "Why 7:45 Still Works" by Diane Ferris, Maplewood Transportation Director

(1) I understand that early mornings can be hard. But moving the start time would cause serious problems.

(2) Maplewood's 14 buses each make two trips: one for the elementary schools and one for the middle and high schools. If elementary school started an hour later, the district would need 9 more buses and drivers. According to the district budget office, that would cost about $480,000 a year.

(3) A later start would also mean a later end. Students would get home after 4:00, leaving less daylight for sports and play in the winter. In a survey of 600 Maplewood families, 61 percent said a later end time would make it harder for them to pick up their children.

(4) There are cheaper ways to help tired students, such as earlier bedtimes and less screen time at night.
questions.stem: How do the two authors try to persuade readers differently?
options: Jonah mostly quotes the district budget office; Ms. Ferris mostly asks readers questions to think about.
Both authors mostly tell stories about their own families to make readers feel sorry for them.
Jonah mostly helps readers feel how tired students are; Ms. Ferris mostly uses costs and survey numbers.
Jonah mostly uses survey results from families; Ms. Ferris mostly describes her own tiring mornings at home.
questions.why: Jonah describes heavy eyes and swimming words, while Ms. Ferris relies on the $480,000 cost and the 61 percent survey result. Each author leans on a different kind of support.

Dear Members of the Cedar Falls Town Council,

(1) Last summer, my family went camping at Lost Pine Lake, two hours away from town. When the campfire went out, I looked up and gasped. The sky was so full of stars that it looked like someone had spilled sugar across a black tablecloth. Back home in Cedar Falls, I can count the stars I see from my backyard on two hands. I am writing to ask the council to change the lights on our streets so that every child in our town can see a sky like that.

(2) Our streetlights shine light in every direction, including straight up into the sky, where no one needs it. Covered lights, called "shielded" lights, point the light down at the sidewalk instead. Mr. Arturo Diaz, who has led the Cedar Falls Astronomy Club for 30 years, says, "With shielded lights, our town could see five times as many stars on a clear night."

(3) Shielded lights save money, too. When the town of Brook Valley switched 800 streetlights to shielded LED lights in 2023, its yearly electric bill for streetlights dropped from $210,000 to $96,000, according to the Brook Valley Public Works Office.

(4) Bright lights at night also confuse animals. Baby sea turtles, for example, crawl toward lights instead of toward the ocean. Even though we don't have sea turtles here, our owls, moths, and bats need the dark too.

(5) Some people worry that shielded lights will make streets less safe. But shielded lights still light up sidewalks and roads, the places people actually walk and drive. They simply stop wasting light on the sky.

(6) Please vote to replace our streetlights with shielded lights. Let's give the stars back to Cedar Falls.

Sincerely,
Nadia Kareem, Grade 4, Cedar Falls Elementary

questions.passage:
Dear Members of the Cedar Falls Town Council,

(1) Last summer, my family went camping at Lost Pine Lake, two hours away from town. When the campfire went out, I looked up and gasped. The sky was so full of stars that it looked like someone had spilled sugar across a black tablecloth. Back home in Cedar Falls, I can count the stars I see from my backyard on two hands. I am writing to ask the council to change the lights on our streets so that every child in our town can see a sky like that.

(2) Our streetlights shine light in every direction, including straight up into the sky, where no one needs it. Covered lights, called "shielded" lights, point the light down at the sidewalk instead. Mr. Arturo Diaz, who has led the Cedar Falls Astronomy Club for 30 years, says, "With shielded lights, our town could see five times as many stars on a clear night."

(3) Shielded lights save money, too. When the town of Brook Valley switched 800 streetlights to shielded LED lights in 2023, its yearly electric bill for streetlights dropped from $210,000 to $96,000, according to the Brook Valley Public Works Office.

(4) Bright lights at night also confuse animals. Baby sea turtles, for example, crawl toward lights instead of toward the ocean. Even though we don't have sea turtles here, our owls, moths, and bats need the dark too.

(5) Some people worry that shielded lights will make streets less safe. But shielded lights still light up sidewalks and roads, the places people actually walk and drive. They simply stop wasting light on the sky.

(6) Please vote to replace our streetlights with shielded lights. Let's give the stars back to Cedar Falls.

Sincerely,
Nadia Kareem, Grade 4, Cedar Falls Elementary

It shows what the town is missing, which gives "give the stars back" its feeling
questions.why: The "spilled sugar" image makes readers feel the wonder of a starry sky. When the letter ends with "give the stars back," readers remember that image and feel the loss.

Text 1: "Uniforms Bring Us Together" by Gloria Fenn, Fernwood parent

(1) Two years ago, my daughter came home in tears. A classmate had laughed at her sneakers because they were not a popular brand. She begged me to buy expensive shoes we could not afford. No eight-year-old should feel ashamed of what her family can buy.

(2) School uniforms would end moments like that. When everyone wears the same navy shirt and khaki pants, no one is judged by labels. Students can focus on who their classmates are, not what they wear.

(3) Principal Raymond Ortiz, who led Oak Hill Elementary for ten years after it switched to uniforms, told the Fernwood Gazette, "I saw students stop comparing clothes and start comparing ideas." Many teachers I have spoken with feel the same way.

(4) Picture our hallways full of students who look like one team. Imagine the pride our children would feel walking into a school where everyone belongs. Let's give them that gift.

Text 2: "Let Our Clothes Speak" by Theo Park, Grade 5

(1) Uniforms are supposed to solve problems, but the facts tell a different story.

(2) First, uniforms are not cheap. The Fernwood Parent Council priced the required uniform at $180 per child for the school year. Most families would still need to buy regular clothes for weekends, so uniforms add a cost instead of replacing one.

(3) Second, uniforms do not stop teasing. When the Fernwood School Board surveyed 12 nearby schools, students at schools with uniforms reported about the same amount of teasing as students at schools without them. Kids who want to tease will find something else to tease about, like haircuts or backpacks.

(4) Finally, choosing our clothes lets us show who we are. My friend Lila wears a different pair of handmade earrings every day. Her clothes tell people she is creative.

(5) Before we spend families' money on a rule, we should make sure it works. The numbers say it doesn't.

options: Fenn's, because it describes a real child whose feelings were badly hurt
Park's, because it describes a friend who shows her creativity with earrings
Park's, because it uses survey results and prices more than personal stories
Fenn's, because it asks readers to imagine the pride students would feel
questions.why: This board member wants proof of results, and Park offers a survey of 12 schools and a real price. Fenn's strongest moments appeal to feelings, which would matter less to this reader.

questions.passageTitle: Uniforms at Westlake? Two Letters to the Editor
questions.passage:
Letter A: "Uniforms Bring Us Together" by Marcus Bell, parent
(1) As a parent of two Westlake Middle School students, I urge the school board to adopt uniforms next fall. Last year, the Westlake Family Survey found that 64 percent of families spend more than $300 each fall on new school clothes. A uniform set of three shirts and two pairs of pants would cost about $120 at Dalton's Outfitters.
(2) Uniforms also reduce pressure. Westlake counselor Rita Gomez, who has worked with middle schoolers for fourteen years, reports that clothing is one of the most common reasons students come to her upset about teasing. "When everyone dresses alike, there's one less thing to be judged for," she says.
(3) Finally, Brookfield Middle School across the county switched to uniforms three years ago. Its principal reports that discipline referrals dropped by 20 percent the following year, though the school also hired two new hall monitors that same year.
(4) Uniforms are a simple, affordable way to help every student feel that they belong.

Letter B: "Let Our Clothes Speak" by Priya Nair, Grade 6
(1) I am a sixth grader at Westlake, and I believe uniforms would take away something important: the chance to show who we are.
(2) Every morning, I choose a shirt with a planet on it, because I want to be an astronaut. My friend Jada wears the bright scarves her grandmother knits for her. When I see her scarf, I think of the love sewn into every stitch. A uniform would fold all of that away into a drawer.
(3) Imagine walking down a hallway where everyone looks exactly the same. Is that a school, or a factory?
(4) Teasing is a real problem, but it won't disappear with matching shirts. Kids who want to tease will find something else—shoes, backpacks, haircuts. What stops teasing is teaching kindness, not hiding differences.
(5) Please let us keep the one way many of us express ourselves every single day.
questions.stem: How do the two authors mainly try to persuade readers differently?
options: Both rely mainly on experts, but the experts Nair quotes are her friends and her classmates.
Bell tells personal stories about his own children; Nair quotes the school counselor's views.
Bell relies mostly on his own feelings; Nair relies mostly on survey results and statistics.
Bell relies mostly on costs, data, and an expert; Nair relies mostly on stories and feelings.
questions.why: Bell uses a survey, prices, a counselor, and another school's results, appealing to reason and authority. Nair uses her planet shirt, Jada's scarves, and a vivid question to appeal to emotion.

Dear Principal Haddad,

(1) Do you remember how much fun it is to win a game of checkers? Our class does! Last year, Board Game Club met every Thursday after lunch. This year, the club is gone, and many students miss it.

(2) Board games are more than fun. They teach us to take turns, follow rules, and plan ahead. When we play chess, we have to think three moves ahead before we act. Isn't that the kind of thinking school is supposed to teach?

(3) Mr. Owens, our art teacher, has offered to watch the club in his room. The Parent Group gave us twelve new games last spring, so the club would not cost the school anything.

(4) Could you tell us by next Friday whether the club can start again? We would be happy to meet with you to talk about it.

Sincerely,
Ms. Lin's Fourth-Grade Class

options: It shows that the class does not know the answer.
It tells her how many games the club owns now.
It leads her to agree that games help students learn.
It explains which teacher will watch the club in the art room.
questions.why: The question nudges the principal to agree that the thinking games teach belongs in school, which supports bringing the club back.

Dear Principal Grant,

(1) How many water bottles, jackets, and lunch boxes does it take to fill a closet? At Pine Hill Middle School, the answer is about three hundred. That is how many items were sitting in our lost-and-found closet last month, according to the school office.

(2) The problem is simple. Students do not have time to dig through a messy closet between classes, so most items are never claimed. At the end of each term, they are donated or thrown away.

(3) I am writing to ask that our school post photos of lost items on the school website each week. Families could look at the pictures at home and email the office if they spot something. Student council volunteers have already offered to take the photos.

(4) This plan would cost nothing, save families money, and keep useful items out of the trash. Isn't it better for a jacket to go home with its owner than to end up in a landfill?

(5) Please let us try this plan for one term and see how many items find their way home.

Sincerely,
Maya Okafor, Grade 6

Dear Principal Haddad,

(1) Do you remember the first book you could read all by yourself? Most people remember that proud moment for the rest of their lives. I am writing to ask you to start a Reading Buddies program at Westbrook Elementary.

(2) In a Reading Buddies program, each fifth grader would meet with a first grader once a week to read together. Our librarian, Ms. Okafor, says that young readers practice more when an older student is cheering them on.

(3) Fifth graders would gain something too. Reading aloud helps us speak clearly and with confidence. It also teaches us patience and kindness.

(4) The program would not cost anything. We already have plenty of books in the library and twenty minutes on Friday afternoons for quiet reading. Why not use that time to help someone else?

(5) Who could say no to a first grader holding up a book and saying, "I read it all by myself"? Please give Reading Buddies a chance.

Sincerely,
Lina Mansour, Grade 5

It changes the topic from cost to the benefits of reading aloud.
It asks the principal to choose a better day for the program.
questions.why: The facts remove the usual reasons to refuse, and the question then points out that there is nothing left stopping the principal from agreeing.

(5) Why should students spend their mornings yawning instead of learning? Let's ask the school board to start our day at 8:30.

questions.passageTitle: Bread Is Not a Duck Treat
questions.passage:
To the Editor of the Brookside Bulletin:

(1) Every Saturday, families gather at Willow Pond to toss bread to the ducks. The children laugh, the ducks quack, and everyone seems happy. But is bread really a treat for a duck?

(2) According to the Willow County Nature Center, bread fills a duck's stomach without giving it the nutrients it needs. Young ducks that eat too much bread can grow weak, bent wings. Bread that sinks also rots in the water, which helps green slime called algae spread across the pond.

(3) Last spring, park workers pulled more than 30 bags of soggy bread out of Willow Pond. Would anyone want to swim in water like that? The ducks have no choice.

(4) There are better ways to enjoy the ducks. Cracked corn, frozen peas, and oats are safer foods. Even better, families can simply watch the ducks dive and paddle.

(5) I have one question for the Parks Department: Could you put up a sign near the pond that lists safe duck foods? A sign would teach families what to bring before they arrive.

(6) Every one of us loves these ducks. Don't the birds of Willow Pond deserve food that keeps them strong and healthy?

Priya Nair, Grade 4, Brookside Elementary
questions.stem: How does the question at the end of the letter help drive home the author's point?
options: It brings up a new problem about the pond's sign.
It leaves readers agreeing that ducks should get healthy food.
It shows that the author has changed her mind about bread.
It asks readers to guess how many ducks live in Willow Pond each year.
questions.why: The final question expects the answer "yes," so readers finish the letter agreeing with the main message: ducks need healthy food, not bread.

(1) When was the last time you saw the Milky Way? If you live in Elmwood, the honest answer may be "never." Bright streetlights, glowing signs, and parking-lot lamps fill our night sky with an orange haze that hides all but the brightest stars.

(2) This kind of light pollution is more than a problem for stargazers. Scientists have found that bright night lighting confuses migrating birds, which use the stars to find their way. Sea turtles, moths, and bats are affected too. Many people also sleep poorly when outdoor light shines through their windows all night.

(3) The good news is that light pollution is one of the easiest kinds of pollution to fix. Shielded lights point downward, lighting the sidewalk instead of the sky. Motion sensors turn lights on only when someone is there. According to the Elmwood Public Works Department, switching the town's 1,200 streetlights to shielded LED fixtures would cut the town's lighting bill by about 40 percent.

(4) Some residents worry that darker streets will be less safe. However, shielded lights still light the ground; they simply stop wasting light by sending it upward, where it helps no one. In fact, glare from unshielded bulbs can make it harder for drivers to see.

(5) Towns across the country, such as Flagstaff, Arizona, have passed "dark sky" rules and still keep their streets well lit. If they can protect their night sky, why can't we?

(6) The town council will vote on a new lighting rule next month. Attend the meeting, write to your council member, and help Elmwood see the stars again.

options: It asks readers to research why Flagstaff decided to pass its rules.
It shows that Flagstaff has darker streets that are less safe at night.
It uses Flagstaff's success to suggest Elmwood has no good excuse not to act.
It suggests Elmwood should hire Flagstaff's workers to change all of its lights.
questions.why: Since Flagstaff protected its sky and kept streets well lit, the question "why can't we?" implies Elmwood can and should do the same.

Dear Principal Haddad,

(1) Walk down the main hallway of Cedar Grove Middle School, and what do you see? Beige walls, a few faded posters, and a fire extinguisher. Is this really the best we can offer the 640 students who walk these halls every day?

(2) Our art club would like to paint a mural on the long wall outside the gym. The design would show the history of Cedar Grove, from the farms that once covered this land to the river trail that families use today. Every student would be invited to submit ideas, and the club would choose a final design with help from Ms. Bell, our art teacher.

(3) A mural would do more than brighten a wall. When students help create something, they feel that the school belongs to them, and students who feel connected to their school are more likely to take care of it. The Cedar Grove PTA has offered to donate $400 for paint and supplies, and Benson's Hardware has promised brushes and drop cloths.

(4) Some teachers may worry that painting will interrupt classes. The club would work only after school and on two Saturdays, so no class time would be lost. When the mural is finished, a clear coating would protect it from scuffs for years.

(5) Three other middle schools in our county already have student murals. Why should Cedar Grove students settle for blank walls? We are ready to plan, paint, and clean up after ourselves. All we need is your permission.

Sincerely,
The Cedar Grove Art Club

questions.passage:
(1) Good evening. Every morning at 8:05, the speaker in our classroom crackles, and an adult voice reads the lunch menu and the weather. Who among us remembers a single word of it by 8:10?

(2) I am here to ask the committee to let fifth graders read the morning announcements. At Hilltop Elementary across town, students have read the announcements since 2023. Their principal, Mrs. Grace Lin, told our class that students now listen more closely because they want to hear their friends.

(3) Some people worry that students will make mistakes. That is a fair concern. That is why our plan includes a practice session every Thursday with our music teacher, Mr. Alvarez, who has trained student speakers for school concerts for twelve years. Each reader would also use a written script approved by the office.

(4) Speaking in front of others is a skill we will need all our lives. We will give reports in middle school, interview for jobs, and maybe even speak at meetings like this one. Where better to practice than in a place where everyone knows our names?

(5) Our plan is ready. We have a schedule, a teacher to train us, and forty students who have already signed up. The only thing missing is your yes. So I will end with one question: if not now, when?

- Speech by Tariq Nasser, Grade 5, to the Parent-Teacher Committee

questions.passageTitle: Let the Stars Shine Over Miller Park
questions.passage:
(1) When was the last time you looked up at night and saw the Milky Way? Many children in Brookfield have never seen it at all.

(2) Last fall, the town installed twelve new floodlights in Miller Park. The lights are so bright that they glow all night, even when the park is empty. The Brookfield Astronomy Club measured the night sky before and after the lights went in. Members found that the number of stars visible from the park dropped from about 300 to fewer than 40.

(3) Bright lights do more than hide stars. Scientists at the Brookfield Nature Center explain that many birds migrate at night and use starlight to find their way. Glowing lights can confuse them. Moths and other insects circle the lights until they are worn out. Should a park meant for nature really be harming the creatures that live in it?

(4) What would the fix cost? Very little. The council could put shields on the lights so they point down and add timers that switch them off at 10 p.m., when the park closes. Nearby Carver Township did exactly this in 2024, and its town office reports saving about $2,000 a year on electricity.

(5) Children deserve to look up and wonder. Isn't a sky full of stars worth a few light shields? The town council meets on May 6. Let council members know you want the stars back.

- Editorial, The Brookfield Weekly

It weighs a big benefit against a small cost.
questions.why: The question compares something wonderful (a starry sky) with something small (a few shields), leading readers to agree that the fix is worth it.

questions.passageTitle: Seat Belts on Every School Bus
questions.passage:
(1) Good evening, members of the Ridgeway School Board. My name is Carlos Mendes, and I am a sixth grader at Ridgeway Middle School. Every morning, I ride Bus 14 for twenty-five minutes along Route 9, a busy highway with a speed limit of 55 miles per hour.

(2) When we get into a car, we buckle up without thinking. Our parents would never drive us to school without seat belts. So why do we accept riding to school without them every single day?

(3) I know that school buses are already very safe. They are large, bright yellow, and built with high, padded seats that protect riders in many crashes. However, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has stated that lap-and-shoulder belts add extra protection, especially in rollovers and side crashes. Several states, including California and Texas, now require seat belts on new school buses.

(4) Adding belts would cost money. The Ridgeway transportation office estimates about $10,000 per bus. That is a real cost. But what price would any of us put on a child's safety? A new bus lasts around twelve years, so the cost works out to less than $900 a year per bus.

(5) Belts also help in another way. Drivers in districts with belts report that students stay seated and behave better, so drivers can keep their eyes on the road.

(6) Some people say students will not wear the belts. Isn't that a reason to teach students, not a reason to give up? We learned to buckle up in cars, and we can learn to buckle up on buses.

(7) I am asking the board to require seat belts on every new bus Ridgeway buys, starting next year. We buckle up everywhere else. Shouldn't the ride to school be just as safe?
questions.stem: How does the question in paragraph 6 respond to people who think students will not wear the belts?
options: It turns the worry into a reason to teach students rather than give up.
It shows that drivers, not students, should be responsible for belts.
It agrees that students will refuse belts, so the plan should be dropped.
It proves with data that every student already wears a seat belt.
questions.why: The question suggests that students not wearing belts is a problem teaching can solve, which takes away the force of the objection.

(1) Would you eat your lunch off the floor of the school bus? Of course not. Yet many of us do something almost as risky every day: we eat with hands that have barely been washed.

(2) Last month, our health class watched students at the sinks for one week. They found that most students washed for about five seconds, and nearly half skipped the soap. Health experts recommend scrubbing with soap for at least twenty seconds.

(3) Why does twenty seconds matter? Soap needs time to loosen the oils on our skin that germs cling to. A quick rinse simply moves the germs around.

(4) I know what some of you are thinking: who has time for that when lunch is waiting? But twenty seconds is about how long it takes to hum "Happy Birthday" twice. You spend longer than that standing in the lunch line.

(5) Last winter, Room 12 tried a handwashing challenge for a month. Their teacher reported that absences in her class dropped by almost a third compared with the month before. Isn't a little extra scrubbing worth more days with your friends and fewer days sick in bed?

(6) Starting next week, every sink will have a timer sticker. Scrub until it turns green. Your hands, and your classmates, will thank you.

- Nurse Carmen Ortiz, Oakdale Elementary Health Blog

(1) Who wants to spend winter break sick in bed? Not you, and not me. Luckily, there is a simple way to fight germs, and it is already in every bathroom at Oakdale School: soap and water.

(2) Germs are too tiny to see, but they are everywhere. They ride on doorknobs, pencils, and lunch trays. When we touch our eyes, nose, or mouth, germs can get inside our bodies. Washing our hands removes many of them before that happens.

(3) The trick is time. Many students splash water on their hands for three seconds and run off. Health experts say we should scrub with soap for at least twenty seconds. That is about as long as singing "Happy Birthday" twice.

(4) Last winter, our office kept track of sick days. In February, the two classes that practiced handwashing before lunch had about half as many absences as the other classes. Why would we ignore a habit that works that well?

(5) Some students have asked me, "Do I need to wash if my hands look clean?" Yes! Germs can hide on hands that look perfectly clean.

(6) So the next time you head to the sink, slow down and hum a tune. Aren't twenty seconds worth a winter full of fun?

— Nurse Carla Benson, Oakdale School Health Blog

(1) Every evening, the bakery on Marlowe Avenue throws away bread that was baked that morning. Every week, the farmers' market packs up crates of bruised but perfectly good apples. Meanwhile, the Marlowe Food Pantry reports that it served 1,900 families last year, up from 1,300 the year before. How can a town with so much extra food also have so many hungry neighbors?

(2) A community fridge could help solve both problems. A community fridge is a refrigerator placed outdoors, usually under a small shelter, where anyone can leave fresh food and anyone can take what they need. There are no forms and no lines.

(3) Our youth council has studied fridges in other towns. In Brookfield, a single fridge outside the library gives away about 300 pounds of food each week, according to the volunteers who run it. Local businesses donate leftovers, and families stop by on their way home.

(4) A fridge would also cut down on waste. The Marlowe Sanitation Department estimates that food makes up nearly a third of what residents throw away each week. Every loaf of bread that is shared is one less loaf hauled to the landfill.

(5) We have a plan. The Marlowe Community Center has agreed to host the fridge beside its front entrance, where there is power and a security camera. A volunteer team would clean it every day and remove anything spoiled. The health department has given us a list of food-safety rules to post on the door.

(6) Some people ask, "Won't people just take everything?" In Brookfield, volunteers say that food is usually taken by people who need it, and the fridge is refilled within hours. Even if items disappear quickly, isn't that exactly what the fridge is for?

(7) The fridge itself will cost about $1,200, including the shelter. What is $1,200 compared with tons of wasted food and hundreds of families going without?

(8) Join us at the Community Center on Saturday to help build the shelter. Bring a hammer, bring a friend, and bring your appetite for change.

questions.passageTitle: Field Trips or Virtual Tours? Two Views
questions.passage:
Text A: "Keep Real Field Trips" by Ana Lindqvist

(1) Can a screen really replace the smell of a pine forest or the roar of a waterfall? Can a video let you touch a fossil or feel the cold spray of a river? Of course not. Yet our district is considering replacing most field trips with virtual tours.

(2) Real trips teach in ways a screen cannot. When students visit a museum, they ask questions of real experts and notice details no camera would show. Don't we all remember the trips we took far better than any lesson we watched?

(3) Field trips also give some students their first chance to see places beyond our town. For a child who has never left Westfield, one day at the science museum can spark a lifelong interest. How could a video on a classroom screen ever do the same?

(4) Some people say trips cost too much. But shouldn't the experiences that matter most be the last things we cut? Are we really willing to let a budget decide what wonder is worth?

(5) Let's keep our buses rolling and our students exploring.

Text B: "Virtual Tours Can Take Us Further" by Devin Shah

(1) Why should a student's zip code decide which museums she can visit? Right now, it does. Last year, the Westfield School District spent $62,000 on field-trip buses, according to the district budget office, and most trips went no farther than forty miles.

(2) Virtual tours change that. For about $150 per class, students can tour the Smithsonian, explore a coral reef with a marine biologist, or talk with an astronaut. A pilot program at two Westfield schools last spring found that 81 percent of students said they learned "a lot" or "quite a lot" from their virtual visits.

(3) Virtual tours also solve practical problems. There are no permission slips lost in backpacks, no chaperones to find, and no class time lost on long bus rides. Students who cannot travel because of health needs can join every tour with their classmates. Isn't that a fairer way to learn?

(4) I am not saying real trips have no value. Students should still take one in-person trip each year. But if we can reach the whole world for a fraction of the cost, why would we limit ourselves to the places a bus can reach in an hour?

(5) Let's spend our money where it reaches the most students.

questions.passageTitle: Give Bats a Home in Hollis Park
questions.passage:
(1) What flies through Hollis Park every summer night, eats thousands of insects, and asks for nothing in return? If you guessed "bats," you are right, and they need our help.

(2) A single little brown bat can eat as many as 1,000 mosquito-sized insects in an hour, according to the Hollis Nature Center. Farmers across the country save billions of dollars each year because bats eat crop-destroying pests. Who wouldn't want a free, all-natural bug control service?

(3) Yet our local bats are losing their homes. Last fall, the park department removed six old, hollow trees near the pond for safety reasons. Those trees were the bats' favorite roosting spots. Nature Center volunteers counted 140 bats leaving the pond area at dusk in 2024; this summer, they counted only 52.

(4) Our class is proposing a simple solution: install ten bat houses on poles around the pond. Each house costs about $60 to build, and our class has already raised $350 through a bake sale. The Nature Center has agreed to show us the best locations.

(5) Bat houses work. When the town of Greenvale put up eight bat houses near its lake in 2021, bats were using six of them within two summers, according to a report from the Greenvale Parks Department. Why wouldn't the same thing happen here, where bats already live?

(6) Some neighbors fear bats. Aren't bats dirty, scary creatures that tangle in people's hair? This is a myth. Bats use echolocation to avoid objects as thin as a human hair, and they almost never fly close to people. Isn't it time we stopped believing old stories and started looking at the facts?

(7) Besides, haven't bats been part of Hollis for as long as anyone can remember? Doesn't everyone love seeing them swoop over the pond on summer evenings? Surely nobody wants the park to be silent at night.

(8) Please support our proposal at the Parks Committee meeting on May 3. The bats can't speak for themselves, so let's speak for them.
questions.stem: How does the tone set by the riddle-like question in paragraph 1 change by paragraph 3?
options: It shifts from serious concern to playful jokes about bats tangling in people's hair.
It stays playful throughout, since the editorial never presents a real problem.
It shifts from friendly interest to anger at the neighbors who fear bats.
It shifts from playful curiosity to serious concern about the falling bat count.
questions.why: The opening riddle invites readers in lightly, but paragraph 3 turns serious with the drop from 140 bats to 52 after the trees were removed.
