(1) Dear Members of the Greenfield City Council,
My name is Hana Kim, and I am a fifth grader at Harper Road Elementary. Every school day, about 150 students walk along Harper Road. On the stretch between Oak Lane and our school, there is no sidewalk at all, only a narrow dirt edge beside fast-moving cars.

(2) Would any of you let your own child walk along the edge of a busy road? I do not think you would. Yet that is what we do every morning.

(3) The danger is real. The Greenfield Police Department recorded 14 near-misses involving walkers on Harper Road last year. A county traffic study found that cars on this road travel an average of 38 miles per hour, even though the speed limit near the school is 25. Last October, a second grader slipped off the dirt edge into the road. Luckily, the driver stopped in time.

(4) Some council members have said a sidewalk would cost too much. What would a sidewalk really cost the city? The city's engineering office estimates that a sidewalk along the half-mile stretch would cost $210,000. That is a lot of money. However, the state's Safe Routes to School program pays up to 80 percent of the cost of sidewalks near schools, which would lower the city's share to about $42,000.

(5) Don't you care about kids at all? Families in our neighborhood have asked for this sidewalk for six years.

(6) A sidewalk would not just protect students. Neighbors could walk their dogs, push strollers, and jog safely. Parents who now drive their children because the road feels unsafe could walk instead, which would mean less traffic at drop-off. What kind of town do we want to be: one that waits for an accident, or one that prevents it?

Sincerely,
Hana Kim

options: It offers only two choices, making the sidewalk seem responsible.
It suggests that accidents on Harper Road cannot really be prevented.
It asks the council to describe what kind of town Greenfield is today.
It shifts the focus of the letter from student safety to dog walking.
questions.why: By framing the decision as waiting for an accident or preventing one, the question makes building the sidewalk seem like the only sensible choice.

questions.passageTitle: Let Us Measure Our Own Weather
questions.passage:
(1) Members of the board, last March my classmate Omar raised his hand during science and asked, "Why did it rain at our school but not at my grandmother's house two miles away?" Our teacher smiled and said, "Great question. Let's find out." But we couldn't find out, because the nearest weather station is at the county airport, eighteen miles away.

(2) I am asking the board to buy a weather station for the roof of Lakeview Elementary. A basic station measures temperature, rainfall, wind speed, and humidity, and it sends the readings to a classroom computer every five minutes.

(3) What would students do with all that data? Quite a lot. Fifth graders could graph rainfall in math class. Fourth graders could compare our temperatures with the airport's. Our school newspaper could print a weekly weather report written by students. We could even share our readings with the local TV station, which asks schools to send in weather reports.

(4) The station would also help with safety. Right now, the office decides whether to hold recess indoors by looking out the window. With a station, the staff could check real wind speeds and storm alerts. Shouldn't safety decisions be based on real measurements, not guesses?

(5) The cost is about $1,400, according to a quote from Summit Science Supply. The Lakeview Parent Club has already offered to pay half. Spread over the 500 students at our school, the board's share works out to $1.40 per student. The company says the station is built to last at least ten years with very little care.

(6) Scientists learn by asking questions and collecting evidence. Isn't that exactly what we want our students to learn? Omar's question deserves an answer. Give us the tools, and we will find it ourselves.

questions.passage:
(1) Members of the board, last March my classmate Omar raised his hand during science and asked, "Why did it rain at our school but not at my grandmother's house two miles away?" Our teacher smiled and said, "Great question. Let's find out." But we couldn't find out, because the nearest weather station is at the county airport, eighteen miles away.

(2) I am asking the board to buy a weather station for the roof of Lakeview Elementary. A basic station measures temperature, rainfall, wind speed, and humidity, and it sends the readings to a classroom computer every five minutes.

(3) What would students do with all that data? Quite a lot. Fifth graders could graph rainfall in math class. Fourth graders could compare our temperatures with the airport's. Our school newspaper could print a weekly weather report written by students. We could even share our readings with the local TV station, which asks schools to send in weather reports.

(4) The station would also help with safety. Right now, the office decides whether to hold recess indoors by looking out the window. With a station, the staff could check real wind speeds and storm alerts. Shouldn't safety decisions be based on real measurements, not guesses?

(5) The cost is about $1,400, according to a quote from Summit Science Supply. The Lakeview Parent Club has already offered to pay half. Spread over the 500 students at our school, the board's share works out to $1.40 per student. The company says the station is built to last at least ten years with very little care.

(6) Scientists learn by asking questions and collecting evidence. Isn't that exactly what we want our students to learn? Omar's question deserves an answer. Give us the tools, and we will find it ourselves.

- Speech by Noor Haddad, Grade 5, to the Lakeview School Board

(1) When was the last time you saw the Milky Way? If you live in Pinecrest, you probably can't remember. Our town is so bright at night that most of the stars have disappeared.

(2) Light that shines up into the sky instead of down onto the ground is called light pollution. The Pinecrest Astronomy Club measured the night sky last fall. From the middle of town, members could count only about 40 stars. Twenty miles away, at Bear Lake, they counted more than 2,000.

(3) Lost stars are not the only problem. Scientists have found that bright lights at night confuse animals. Baby sea turtles on beaches crawl toward street lights instead of the ocean. Birds that travel at night can fly in circles around lit-up buildings until they are too tired to go on. Do we really want our lights to harm the animals we share the world with?

(4) The good news is that the fix is simple. Shielded lights point down at the sidewalk, where people need them, instead of up at the sky. Motion-sensor lights turn on only when someone walks by. The town of Ridgeview switched to shielded street lights two years ago and says its electric bill dropped by about one-fifth.

(5) Some people ask, "Will darker streets be less safe?" Not if the lights are aimed well. Shielded lights still light the ground; they just stop wasting light upward.

(6) The Pinecrest Town Council will vote on new lighting rules on March 3. Why should our children grow up thinking the sky holds only forty stars?

— The Editorial Board, The Pinecrest Weekly

"Would you want to lose your way home because someone left a light on?"

questions.passageTitle: Lockers for Fifth Graders? Two Views
questions.passage:
Text 1: Our Backs Need a Break
by Maya, Grade 5

(1) Have you ever tried to carry a heavy backpack up three flights of stairs? Every morning, fifth graders at Ridgeway School haul everything they own from class to class: binders, library books, gym shoes, and a lunch box. Some of us carry books in our arms because our bags are too full to zip. By the end of the day, our shoulders ache.

(2) Lockers would change that. We could leave our gym shoes and extra books in a safe place and carry only what we need. Middle schoolers get lockers, so why should we have to wait? We are old enough to remember a combination.

(3) Imagine walking to class with a light bag and a clear mind. Wouldn't every student learn better without a sore back?

Text 2: Lockers Are Not the Answer
by Ben, Grade 5

(1) Lockers sound like a great idea, but would they really solve the problem? Ridgeway's hallways are already crowded. The school's facilities manager, Ms. Patel, says that adding lockers for 120 fifth graders would narrow the main hallway by almost three feet.

(2) Lockers are also expensive. The district budget office estimates that they would cost about $18,000. Our fifth-grade classrooms already have cubbies, and teachers could let us leave heavy books in them overnight for free. Students would also need extra time between classes to stop at their lockers, which means less time for learning.

(3) The real problem is heavy backpacks, not a lack of lockers. Why spend $18,000 when a free solution is already sitting in our classrooms?
questions.stem: How do the two authors use questions differently to persuade readers?
options: Maya's questions point to costs, while Ben's ask readers to picture feelings.
Both authors use questions only at the start to grab the reader's attention.
Maya asks real questions she answers later, while Ben avoids questions.
Maya's questions ask readers to imagine feelings; Ben's point toward facts.
questions.why: Maya asks readers to picture sore shoulders and a light bag, while Ben's questions lead readers to think about hallway space and the $18,000 cost.

(1) Every school day at 7:15 a.m., before most of us are awake enough to talk, Mr. Alvarez is already waiting at the corner of Hill Road. The door of Bus 6 is open, and he is smiling.

(2) Mr. Alvarez has driven Bus 6 for eleven years. He knows every rider's name. He knows that Lucy gets carsick, so he saves her a seat up front. When it snowed in January, he drove the whole route slowly and carefully, and every student arrived safely.

(3) Mr. Alvarez is not the only one. Our school has nine bus drivers, and together they drive about 600 miles every school day, according to the district transportation office. They check tires and brakes before sunrise, and they wait patiently in the cold when a rider is running late.

(4) Our bus drivers do one of the most important jobs at our school. They are the first adults we see each morning and the last we see each afternoon. Yet how often do we stop to thank them?

(5) I am asking the Student Council to create Bus Driver Thank-You Day on April 18. Students could make cards, and the art club could paint a banner for the bus lot. The Parent Group has offered to bring breakfast for the drivers.

(6) Last week, some council members asked me, "Who will pay for the banner?" The art club already has paint and paper left over from the fall fair, so the banner will cost nothing.

(7) A thank-you card takes ten minutes to make. Mr. Alvarez has given us eleven years. Isn't it time we gave something back?

— Speech by Jada Thompson, Grade 4 Student Council Representative

Text 1: "Uniforms Make Mornings Easier," a speech by Hannah Cole

(1) How much time did you spend this morning deciding what to wear? For many students at Lakeview Elementary, the answer is "too much." A school uniform would solve that problem.

(2) With uniforms, every student wears the same simple outfit: navy pants or a navy skirt with a white or light blue shirt. No one has to worry about whether their clothes are new or in style. Wouldn't it be nice if nobody got teased about a shirt ever again?

(3) Uniforms can also save families money. The Lakeview Parent Group found that a set of five uniform shirts costs about $35, which is less than many brand-name shirts.

(4) Let's make our school a place where people notice who we are, not what we wear.

Text 2: "Let Us Choose," a speech by Omar Siddiqi

(1) Our clothes tell people about us. My red running shoes show that I love to race. My friend's dinosaur shirt shows everyone that she dreams of becoming a scientist someday. Clothes are one way students share who they are.

(2) Supporters say uniforms stop teasing. But students who want to tease will just pick on backpacks or haircuts instead. Our dress code already bans rude words and pictures, and it keeps our school respectful.

(3) Uniforms also mean buying a whole second set of clothes. Many families already have plenty of shirts and pants at home that fit just fine.

(4) When will we ever learn to make good choices if adults make every choice for us?

Text 1: "Uniforms Make Mornings Easier," a speech by Hannah Cole

(1) How much time did you spend this morning deciding what to wear? For many students at Lakeview Elementary, the answer is "too much." A school uniform would solve that problem.

(2) With uniforms, every student wears the same simple outfit: navy pants or a navy skirt with a white or light blue shirt. No one has to worry about whether their clothes are new or in style. Wouldn't it be nice if nobody got teased about a shirt ever again?

(3) Uniforms can also save families money. The Lakeview Parent Group found that a set of five uniform shirts costs about $35, which is less than many brand-name shirts.

(4) Let's make our school a place where people notice who we are, not what we wear.

Text 2: "Let Us Choose," a speech by Omar Siddiqi

(1) Our clothes tell people about us. My red running shoes show that I love to race. My friend's dinosaur shirt shows everyone that she dreams of becoming a scientist someday. Clothes are one way students share who they are.

(2) Supporters say uniforms stop teasing. But students who want to tease will just pick on backpacks or haircuts instead. Our dress code already bans rude words and pictures, and it keeps our school respectful.

(3) Uniforms also mean buying a whole second set of clothes. Many families already have plenty of shirts and pants at home that fit just fine.

(4) When will we ever learn to make good choices if adults make every choice for us?
questions.stem: What answer does Omar want listeners to think of for his final question?
options: "We already make enough choices, so clothes do not matter."
"We won't learn to choose well unless we get to practice choosing."
"We should ask the adults at school to make even more of our choices."
"We will learn to choose well once adults pick our clothes."
questions.why: Omar asks when students will learn to choose if adults choose everything; he expects the answer "never," so listeners should conclude that students need to practice making choices like picking their clothes.
